seoTitle: How to Connect MT4 or MT5 to TradingView
metaDescription: Learn how to bridge TradingView with MetaTrader 4 or 5 using broker connections, third-party connectors, and alert-forwarding tools.
intro: TradingView and MetaTrader solve different problems — TradingView is where most traders do their charting and analysis, while MT4 and MT5 remain the execution terminals a lot of brokers still require. The catch is that TradingView doesn't treat MetaTrader as a native broker, so there's no simple toggle that links the two. This guide covers what TradingView's built-in broker connections actually offer, why MetaTrader isn't among them, and how third-party bridge tools fill that specific gap so a TradingView alert can trigger an order in your MT4 or MT5 terminal.

steps.heading: Understand what TradingView's Trading Panel actually connects to
steps.body: Open any chart in TradingView and switch to the Trading Panel tab beneath it — this is where the platform's native broker integrations live. Under "Connect through our trusted brokers" you'll see a grid of options: TradingView's own Paper Trading simulator, then real brokers such as Dhan, Fyers, Interactive Brokers, Alice Blue, Share.Market, and Paytm Money, each with a star rating. This panel is TradingView's real, working bridge to live execution — but MetaTrader isn't one of the listed partners, which is exactly why MT4 and MT5 users need a different route.

image.caption: TradingView's Trading Panel, open to "Connect through our trusted brokers." MetaTrader isn't among the native options, which is the whole reason a bridge tool is necessary.

steps.heading: Confirm your MetaTrader account is broker-ready first
steps.body: Before touching any connector, log into MT4 or MT5 directly and confirm the account is active, funded appropriately for your testing, and connected to a live server through your broker — not just the demo environment. Bridge tools relay signals into whatever terminal session is running, so if MetaTrader itself isn't properly logged in and connected to your broker's server, nothing forwarded from TradingView will have anywhere to land.

steps.heading: Set up alerts inside TradingView
steps.body: Since the direct Trading Panel route doesn't cover MetaTrader, the workaround is TradingView's alert system. From the toolbar, open Alert and build a condition off an indicator, a price level, or a strategy signal exactly as you would for a normal notification. The difference is what happens next: instead of just popping up on your screen, this alert becomes the trigger a bridge service listens for and turns into an order.

image.caption: The TradingView homepage with the product menu open. This is the same account and workspace where alerts get created before being routed out to a bridge service.

steps.heading: Connect a third-party bridge tool
steps.body: Services like PineConnector and comparable webhook-based connectors sit between the two platforms: you point your TradingView alert's webhook URL at the connector, and the connector translates that signal into an order your MT4 or MT5 terminal can execute through an installed expert advisor or script. Setup typically means creating an account with the bridge provider, installing their small MetaTrader-side component, and pasting their webhook address into your TradingView alert configuration. Each tool has its own setup instructions, so follow the provider's current documentation rather than assuming the steps are identical across services.

steps.heading: Match the alert message format the bridge expects
steps.body: Bridge tools parse the text in your TradingView alert message to know what order to place, so the message has to follow the connector's exact syntax — typically something specifying the license key, the action (buy or sell), the symbol, and risk parameters like lot size or stop loss. A message that doesn't match the expected format either gets ignored or, worse, misread into the wrong order, so copy the format from the provider's documentation rather than guessing at it.

steps.heading: Test the full path with a small trade before trusting it
steps.body: Fire a test alert and confirm it appears correctly in your MetaTrader terminal before connecting the bridge to a strategy that trades unattended. Check that the symbol, direction, and size all landed as expected, and watch for any sync delay between the alert firing and the order appearing. Only after a clean test or two should you let the bridge run against a live strategy, since a misconfigured connector can place trades faster than you can catch a mistake.

faq.question: Can TradingView connect directly to MetaTrader without third-party tools?
faq.answer: No. TradingView's native Trading Panel lists brokers like Interactive Brokers, Dhan, and Alice Blue, but MetaTrader isn't among them, so a bridge tool or webhook connector is required to link the two.

faq.question: Is PineConnector free to use?
faq.answer: No, PineConnector and similar bridge services run on their own subscription pricing. Check the provider's current plans before committing to one for live trading.

faq.question: Does this bridge setup work for both MT4 and MT5?
faq.answer: Most bridge and connector tools support both, though the MetaTrader-side installation (expert advisor or script) and exact setup steps can differ slightly between MT4 and MT5.

faq.question: Why doesn't TradingView just support MetaTrader natively?
faq.answer: TradingView's Trading Panel integrates with brokers directly through their own APIs. MetaTrader is a third-party terminal used across many different brokers rather than a single broker itself, which is why it isn't built into TradingView's native broker list.

faq.question: Is connecting TradingView to MetaTrader risky?
faq.answer: It can be if the alert message format or webhook setup is wrong, since a bridge can place live orders automatically. Test thoroughly with a small trade and confirm the symbol, direction, and size match before relying on it for real capital.
